passages.title: The ruined city asks to be seen
passages.summary: Jerusalem sits alone, like a widow who was once a princess. She weeps at night, and none of her friends comfort her. Judah has gone into exile, and no one comes to the feasts. Her enemies prosper, and her children are captives. The poem says she sinned and has been afflicted for it. Then the city speaks for herself. She asks those who pass by to look at her sorrow. She admits she rebelled, and she asks God to see what her enemies have done.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Jerusalem. The poems do not give a continuous travel route.

lds.text: The 2026 Seminary lesson reads this grief alongside the Savior’s compassion. Why does Jerusalem ask travelers to look at her sorrow?

contextNote.title: The ruined city asks to be seen
contextNote.text: For eleven verses a speaker describes Jerusalem as “she.” In verse 12 the city begins to speak as “I.” She calls to strangers on the road, since no one else will listen. The poem says five times that she has no comforter. What she asks first is to be seen. Verse 18 admits that the LORD is right and she rebelled. That admission does not end her cry for help.

passages.title: Prayer rises from the hungry streets
passages.summary: The poem says the Lord has acted like an enemy against Zion. He has thrown down her walls, her palaces, and his own sanctuary. King and priest are rejected, and the prophets receive no vision. Elders sit silent on the ground. The poet’s eyes fail with weeping, because children faint in the streets. Her prophets saw false visions and did not expose her guilt. The poet tells Zion to cry out to the Lord through the night. She asks God to look at whom he has treated this way.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Jerusalem. The poems do not give a continuous travel route.

lds.text: Why does the call to pray focus on hungry children?

contextNote.title: Prayer rises from the hungry streets
contextNote.text: Verses 11–12 describe infants asking their mothers for food and dying. That picture drives the whole poem. Verse 5 says the Lord became “like an enemy.” He is still the only one to turn to. In verse 19 the poet urges Zion to pour out her heart for her children. The prayer she then offers is not gentle. Verse 20 says, “Look, LORD, and see to whom you have done thus.”

passages.title: Hope interrupts grief without ending it
passages.summary: One man speaks of the suffering he has seen under God’s anger. God has walled him in and shut out his prayer. He has become a joke, and his hope from the LORD is gone. Then he calls something to mind and has hope. The LORD’s mercies never end and are new every morning. It is good to wait quietly, for the Lord does not reject forever. He calls the people to examine their ways and return. Then he weeps again, and he asks God to judge his enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Jerusalem. The poems do not give a continuous travel route.

lds.text: The 2026 Seminary lesson connects remembered mercy with the Savior’s willingness to forgive. How does renewed complaint follow the speaker’s remembered mercy?

contextNote.title: Hope interrupts grief without ending it
contextNote.text: Verse 21 stands near the middle of the book. “This” points ahead to verses 22–23. The speaker’s situation has not changed. His hope comes from what he chooses to remember. Verse 33 adds that God does not afflict people willingly. From verse 42 the complaint returns: “you have not pardoned.” Hope interrupts the grief in this poem and does not end it.

passages.title: Failed protection and the cost of hunger
passages.summary: The poet mourns that Zion’s gold has grown dim. Her precious children are treated like clay pots. Infants thirst, and no one gives them bread. Those who ate fine food now lie on trash heaps. The city’s punishment is worse than Sodom’s, which fell in a moment. This came through the sins of her prophets and priests, who shed innocent blood. The people watched in vain for a nation that could not save. Their king, the LORD’s anointed, was captured.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Jerusalem. The poems do not give a continuous travel route.

lds.text: How does the poem connect public leaders with innocent blood?

contextNote.title: Failed protection and the cost of hunger
contextNote.text: The poem names three protections that failed. Prophets and priests, a foreign ally, and the king all failed (verses 13, 17, 20). It begins with the religious leaders. They should have warned the city, and they shed the blood of the just. The starving children of verses 4 and 10 are the cost. Verse 6 says a slow death by hunger is worse than Sodom’s sudden end. Verse 22 sets a limit: Zion’s punishment is complete.

passages.title: A shared prayer ends without an answer
passages.summary: The people ask the LORD to remember what has happened to them. Strangers hold their land and houses. They are orphans, and they must buy their own water and wood. Slaves rule over them, and they risk their lives for bread. Women are abused, princes are hanged, and elders receive no respect. Music has stopped, and Mount Zion lies empty. They say the LORD reigns forever and ask why he forgets them. They ask him to bring them back, unless he has utterly rejected them.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Jerusalem. The poems do not give a continuous travel route.

lds.text: What remains unresolved after the people ask for renewal?

contextNote.title: A shared prayer ends without an answer
contextNote.text: This last poem is a prayer from start to finish. The people say “we” and “us” in every part. Verse 19 says the LORD’s throne stands, though verse 18 shows his hill in ruins. Verse 21 asks God to do the turning. The people do not think they can return on their own. Verse 22 then raises the fear that he has rejected them. The book ends there, with no answer recorded.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Kingdom of Judah · approximate
regions.summary: Judah was the southern kingdom. David’s family ruled it from Jerusalem for about four centuries.
regions.detail: The poems mourn Jerusalem after its fall. Judah has gone into exile (Lamentations 1:3).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It is not a border for one year.

regions.name: Egypt · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
regions.detail: Lamentations 5:6 says the people gave their hand to Egypt and Assyria for bread.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: Lamentations 4:21–22 tells Edom that the cup will pass to her too.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

chapterMaps.narrative: The people ask the LORD to remember what has happened to them. Strangers hold their land and houses. They are orphans, and they must buy their own water and wood. Slaves rule over them, and they risk their lives for bread. Women are abused, princes are hanged, and elders receive no respect. Music has stopped, and Mount Zion lies empty. They say the LORD reigns forever and ask why he forgets them. They ask him to bring them back, unless he has utterly rejected them.
